ISO C++ Core Guidelines — table of contents (extract)
The guidelines are a set of best-practice rules for writing modern,
safe, performant C++. They are organized by topic.

P: Philosophy
- P.1: Express ideas directly in code
- P.2: Write in ISO Standard C++
- P.3: Express intent
- P.4: Ideally, a program should be statically type safe

I: Interfaces
- I.1: Make interfaces explicit
- I.2: Avoid non-const global variables
- I.3: Avoid singletons
- I.4: Make interfaces precisely and strongly typed

F: Functions
- F.1: Package meaningful operations as carefully named functions
- F.2: A function should perform a single logical operation
- F.3: Keep functions short and simple

C: Classes and class hierarchies
- C.1: Organize related data, functions, and overloads into classes
- C.2: Use class if the class has an invariant

ES: Expressions and statements
- ES.1: Prefer the standard library to other libraries
- ES.2: Prefer suitable abstractions to direct use of language features
- ES.5: Keep scopes small
- ES.20: Always initialize an object
- ES.22: Don't declare a variable until you have a value to initialize it with

Per: Performance
- Per.1: Don't optimize without reason
- Per.2: Don't optimize prematurely
- Per.3: Don't optimize through something that's not a bottleneck

CP: Concurrency
- CP.1: Assume that your code will run as part of a multi-threaded program
- CP.2: Avoid data races
- CP.3: Minimize explicit sharing of writable data

Error handling
- E.1: Develop an error-handling strategy early in a design
- E.2: Throw an exception to signal that a function cannot perform its
  assigned task
- E.28: Avoid error handling based on global state
